transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hi Delphine, come in. What's brought you in today?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've been getting these headaches, and they're getting more frequent. I wanted to get them checked.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Of course. How long have you been getting them?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About six months now. Maybe two or three a month.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Can you describe one for me, from the beginning?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It starts with my vision. I get these zigzag lines, shimmering, off to one side.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long do the zigzags last?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About an hour. Actually, no. I timed it last time, and it was twenty minutes, then it went.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's really helpful, twenty minutes. Then what happens?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Then the headache comes. It's on one side, usually the left, and it throbs.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Anything else with it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel sick and I can't stand bright lights. I have to lie down in a dark room.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long does the headache last?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Most of the day. I'm wiped out the next day too.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking with them?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, just the vision thing.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you ever had a sudden, severe headache, like being hit on the head, the worst ever?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Are they worse when you lie down, cough or strain?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any fevers or stiff neck?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Does anyone in the family get migraines?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My mum, but she never gets the lights.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What are you taking for them?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Paracetamol, but it doesn't do much.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any other medicines? Are you on any contraception?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The pill. Rigevidon. I've been on it about four years.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you smoke?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay. Let me check a few things. Your blood pressure is 118 over 76. I'll look at the back of your eyes. Those look normal. Follow my finger. Squeeze my hands. Your nervous system examination is completely normal.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's good.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It is. From what you've described, these are migraines with aura. The zigzags are the aura.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. So is it something serious?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Migraine itself isn't dangerous, but there's one important thing. With migraine with aura, the combined pill increases the risk of stroke, so it isn't safe for you to keep taking it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh. I didn't know that.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd like you to stop the Rigevidon and switch to a progestogen-only pill called desogestrel, 75 micrograms, one every day without a break. It doesn't carry that risk.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. Do I need extra protection?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Yes. Use condoms for the first two days after starting desogestrel.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: For the headaches themselves, I'll prescribe sumatriptan, 50 milligrams. Take it as soon as the headache starts, not during the zigzags. If the headache comes back, you can take another after two hours, but no more than 300 milligrams in 24 hours. You can take it with paracetamol.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: All right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Try not to use painkillers or sumatriptan on more than two or three days a week, because using them too often can actually cause more headaches. Keep a headache diary, and I'll see you in six weeks.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If you get a sudden severe headache, weakness or numbness on one side, difficulty speaking, or a headache with fever and a stiff neck, call 999 or go to A&E.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay, thank you.

reference_note.history: Two to three episodes per month. Preceded by visual aura (shimmering zigzag lines to one side) lasting about 20 minutes. Followed by unilateral, usually left-sided, throbbing headache with nausea and photophobia, lasting most of the day. No focal weakness, numbness or speech disturbance. No thunderclap headache. Not worse on lying down, coughing or straining. No fever or neck stiffness. Mother has migraine without aura. Non-smoker.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Combined oral contraceptive (Rigevidon) for 4 years. Paracetamol as needed. No known drug allergies.
reference_note.examination: BP 118/76. Fundi normal. Neurological examination normal.
reference_note.impression: Migraine with aura. Combined hormonal contraception contraindicated (UKMEC 4).
reference_note.plan: Stop combined pill; start desogestrel 75 micrograms once daily continuously. Use condoms for the first 2 days of desogestrel. Sumatriptan 50 mg at headache onset (not during aura); may repeat after 2 hours, maximum 300 mg in 24 hours; may take with paracetamol. Limit acute treatment to 2–3 days per week to avoid medication-overuse headache. Headache diary. Review in 6 weeks.
reference_note.safety_netting: Call 999 or attend A&E if sudden severe headache, one-sided weakness or numbness, speech difficulty, or headache with fever and neck stiffness.
